Topics 3 heroic tales, 7 cosmology, 9 sacred landscape, 11 taboo. All passages are labeled paraphrase. Chapter X (Old Man of the Mountain) is an invented parable by the author and is excluded.

region.zh: 夏威夷島普納瓦豪拉神廟

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 1 (New York 1915)

summary.en: The heiau Wahaula carried a burning tabu: even its smoke falling on a man was cause for death. The young chief Kahele, journeying around Hawaii, forgets the danger; a wisp of temple smoke touches his cheek, and the temple's body-catcher fells him for the altar. His bones, hidden for dishonorable incantation use, haunt the temple until his ghost flies home to Kau, warns his father in dreams, and guides him through the night to the loose stone behind which the folded bones lie - so the spirit passes to the Under-world in honour.
summary.zh: 瓦豪拉神廟禁忌如焚：連其炊煙落在人身上也是死罪。環遊夏威夷島的青年酋長卡赫勒忘卻此忌，一縷廟煙拂面，廟中『捕人者』揮棒擊倒，獻於祭壇。其骨被折疊收藏、備作邪術之用；幽魂不堪其辱，飛回考烏托夢告其父。父親循跡千里，夜探神廟，移開幽魂所指之石，取回骨束——亡魂遂得尊榮歸入幽冥。

sensitivity.note: Temple-sacrifice legend; paraphrase, no ritual text reproduced.

passages.text: Wahaula was a tabu temple of the very highest rank. The native chants said, concerning this heiau is the burning tabu. The heiau was so thoroughly tabu that the smoke of its fires falling upon any of the people or even upon any one of the chiefs was sufficient cause for punishment by death, with the body as a sacrifice to the gods of the temple. Certain days were tabu to Lono; other days belonged to Ku; at other times Kane was held supreme, then again Kanaloa had his days especially set apart for sacrifice and chant. The Mu, or body-catcher, of this heiau with his assistants seems to have been continually on the watch for human victims, and no one dared rescue a man from his hands, for then the wrath of all the gods would follow him all the days of his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 1 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Many ages ago a young chief named Kahele determined to make a journey around the island visiting all the noted and sacred places. He passed from place to place, riding the surf, gambling, racing the sled, and visiting the most noted of the heiaus. In time he came to Puna, the district in which was located the temple Wahaula. But in the midst of the many stories of the past and the pleasures he had enjoyed, Kahele forgot the peculiar power of the tabu of the smoke of Wahaula. The fierce winds of the south were blowing; he saw the sacred grove and hastened toward the temple. The perilous moment came: the warm breath of one of the fires touched the young chief's cheek, and soon a blow from the club of the Mu laid him senseless on the rough stones. Quickly the body was dismembered and offered as a sacrifice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 1 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: For some reason the priests, after the flesh had decayed, set apart the bones for some special purpose - it may have been that the bones were folded together in the shape known as unihipili, or grasshopper bones, folded and laid away for purposes of incantation, until a new spirit dwelt in the bundle and gave the possessor peculiar power in witchcraft. The spirit of Kahele rebelled against this disposition of all that remained of his body; he wanted to be back in his native district. At last the spirit fled by night from this place of torment to the home he had left. Kahele's father, the high chief of Kau, had a strange dream in which the ghost revealed that he had been put to death and his bones were in danger of dishonorable treatment. The father journeyed secretly around the island, guided by dream-warnings, until he lay down to rest in the lava fields of Wahaula.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 1 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Walking along carelessly to avoid suspicion, he drew near the temple lands and was attacked by an Olohe, a beardless man of a lawless robber clan. Almost all day the battle raged over the lava beds; the chief's well-oiled body was hard to grasp, and at last he forced the Olohe into a narrow place, seized him, broke his bones and killed him. For several days the chief hid himself near the temple, uttering the prayers and incantations needed for the protection of his family gods. One night of very great darkness, when deep sleep rested on all the temple-dwellers, the ghost of Kahele aroused his father for the dangerous task. Step by step he felt his way along the temple walls until the ghost stood near a great rock pointing at a part of the wall. The father seized a stone which very easily was removed from the wall; behind it was a hollow place in which lay a bundle of folded bones. He carried them to Kau and placed them in his own secret family burial cave, and the ghost of Wahaula went down to the spirit world in great joy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 1 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Maluae Descends for the Ghost of His Boy

region.en: Manoa Valley, Oahu, and the breadfruit-tree Lei-walo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦胡島馬諾阿谷與幽冥麵包樹（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 2 (New York 1915)

summary.en: The boy Kaa-lii robs the altars of Kane and Kanaloa; in anger the gods kill him and thrust his ghost into the Under-world. His father Maluae lies refusing food, determined to die with his son; shamed by their own deed, the gods give him a ghost body, a hollow cane of food, weapons and burning lava, and send him down through the ghost-breadfruit-tree of Lei-walo. Battles fought, he finds the boy 'down in the papa-ku' choking on ghost-bananas, and pours the lava-fire of the gods into the floor of Po to drive back the spirits and carry the child's ghost home to its body.
summary.zh: 男孩卡阿利利偷食卡內與卡納洛亞祭壇上的香蕉，二神怒而殺之，將其魂擲入幽冥。父親馬魯埃絕食待死，神自愧過甚，遂授其魂體、內藏食物兵刃與熔岩之火的中空竹杖，令其循幽冥麵包樹萊伊瓦羅而下。父親一路斬鬼開路，終在冥土根基之處尋得噎食鬼蕉的孩童；又傾出神火熔岩，驅散群魂，攜子之魂重返軀體。父子從此終身供奉。

sensitivity.note: Descent-to-underworld cluster: father quests into Po for a child's spirit.

passages.text: In the upper end of Manoa Valley, at the foot of the highest mountains of Oahu, lived Maluae, a farmer, who cultivated bananas and taro and sweet potatoes. Whenever he gathered any food he brought a part to his family temple and placed it on an altar before the gods Kane and Kanaloa. He had a boy whom he dearly loved, Kaa-lii, a careless, rollicking child. One day the boy was tired and hungry; he passed by the temple, saw bananas ripe and sweet on the little platform before the gods, took them and ate them all. The gods looked down expecting food and found nothing; they were very angry, ran out after the boy, caught him eating the bananas and killed him. They left the body under the trees, and taking out his ghost threw it into the Under-world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 2 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The father searched for the body and found it, partly eaten bananas filling the mouth set in death. He wrapped the body in kapa cloth, laid it on the sleeping-mat, refused all food, and planned to die with his boy. The gods talked together, and Kane said: Maluae eats no food, he prepares no awa to drink; he is near the door of the Under-world; if he should die, we would be to blame. Kanaloa said: He has been a good man; we have called him morning and evening in his worship; he has provided fish and fruits and vegetables for our altars; we have not paid him well for his care. So they decided to go and give life to the father, and permit him to take his ghost body and go down into Po, the dark land, to bring back the ghost of the boy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 2 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The gods gave him a ghost body and prepared a hollow stick like bamboo, in which they put food, battle-weapons, and a piece of burning lava for fire. Near the seacoast of Moanalua was a ghostly breadfruit-tree named Lei-walo, perhaps the eighth wreath - the last wreath of leaves from the land of the living which would meet the eyes of the dying. Ghosts would leap or fly or climb into its branches trying to find a rotten branch on which they could sit until it broke and threw them into the dark sea below. Maluae climbed up; his weight broke the branch at once and down they all fell into the land of Po. He tasted the food in his hollow cane for new life and strength, and went from place to place, finding the boy at last 'down in the papa-ku', the established foundation of Po, choking from the bananas of ghost-land which he was compelled to force into his mouth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 2 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The father caught the spirit of the boy and started back toward the Upper-world, but the ghosts surrounded him, trying to take the spirit away. Once more he partook of the food of the gods and wielded his war-club, but the hosts of enemies were too great, multitudes crushing him by overwhelming numbers. At last he raised his magic hollow cane and poured out the portion of burning lava which the gods had placed inside. It fell upon the dry floor of the Under-world; the flames dashed into the trees and shrubs of ghost-land, fire-holes opened in the floor and streams of lava burst out. Backward fled the multitudes of spirits. The father thrust the spirit of the boy quickly into the empty magic cane and rushed swiftly up to his home-land, bringing the spirit to the body lying in the rest-house and forcing it to find again its living home. Afterward the father and the boy took food to the altars of the gods and chanted the accustomed prayers heartily and loyally all the rest of their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 2 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Hau-pu Hurls the Rock of Kauai

region.en: Kaena Point and Pohaku-o-Kauai, Oahu northwest coast
region.zh: 瓦胡島西北岸凱納角與考愛岩

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 3 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Born amid lightning, thunder and blood-rain, the Kauai giant Hau-pu razes armies with spear and torn-up tree. Sleeping across the channel, he wakes to torch-lit fishing on Oahu and, taking the lights for a war fleet, tears a rock from the hillside and hurls it out over the sea. It descends on the fleet of chief Kaena, smashing canoes and killing the chief; the survivors name the new cape Kaena, and the embedded rock rises from the sea as the Rock of Kauai.
summary.zh: 考愛島巨人豪普降生時雷電交加、雨如血色；他一人可掃平千軍。某夜他隔海半醒，聞對岸瓦胡島火光喧鬧，誤以為戰艦來犯，便自山崖拔起巨石奮力擲出。巨石橫越海峽，砸沉漁隊，酋長凱納罹難；部眾以其名命名新海岬，而深嵌海底的巨石則露出水面——即今『考愛島之岩』。

sensitivity.note: Place-name myth for Kaena Point and the offshore rock.

passages.text: Out in the ocean a short distance from the Cape of Kaena lies a large rock which bears the name Pohaku-o-Kauai, the rock of Kauai. A long time ago there lived on the island Kauai a man of wonderful power, by the name of Hau-pu. When he was born the signs of a demi-god were over and around the house of his birth: lightning flashed through the skies, and thunder reverberated; mighty floods of rain carried the red iron soil into the valleys so that the rapids and waterfalls became the color of blood - a blood-rain. A beautiful rainbow rested over the house, thought to come from the miraculous powers of the new-born child; many chiefs throughout the centuries were said to have had this rainbow around them all their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 3 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hau-pu, while a child, was very powerful, and after he grew up was widely known as a great warrior. He would attack and defeat armies of his enemies without aid from any person; if spear and bare hands did not vanquish his foes, he would leap to the hillside, tear up a great tree, and with it sweep away all before him. He became angry quickly and used his great powers very rashly. One night he lay sleeping in his royal rest-house on the side of a mountain facing the island of Oahu across a channel about thirty miles wide. He was aroused by shouts far away, louder, mixed with the roar of the great surf waves, and forced himself to rise and stumble to the door.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 3 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: He looked out toward Oahu: a multitude of lights flashed on the sea, a low murmur of many voices came from the dancing lights, and his confused thoughts made it appear that a great fleet of warriors was coming from Oahu to attack his people. He blindly rushed out to the edge of a high precipice, laughed, stooped down and tore a huge rock from its place, swinging it back and forth until he gave it great impetus which added to his own miraculous power sent it far out over the sea. Over on the shores of Oahu the chief Kaena had called his people out for a night's fishing: torches without number, the largest fish-nets, flashing lights, splashing paddles and clamour from hundreds of voices. Suddenly something like a bird as large as a mountain descended upon them with a mighty roar of winds; smashed and submerged were the canoes when the huge boulder thrown by Hau-pu hurled itself upon them, and Kaena and many of his people lost their lives. The waves swept sand until a long point of land was formed, named Kaena by the remaining followers, and the death-dealing rock, embedded deeply in the ocean bed with its head rising above the waves, was named the Rock of Kauai.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 3 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: The Timid Taro That Flew from the Oven

region.en: South Kona to Kau, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島南科納至考烏

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 4 (New York 1915)

summary.en: In a chief's taro pond above Hookena two plants grew side by side, finer than all the rest, and pledged undying affection. Ordered up for the feast, they moved away, fled patch to patch across all Kona, and at last took wings, flying to Waiohinu, Kau and beyond, pursued by the chief on foot and betrayed by friends and warned by friends. They settled at last under a kindly chief, living to a happy old age as Kalo-eke-eke, the Timid Taro - a myth Westervelt suggests may have grown from the ancient right of subjects to transfer allegiance to a neighbouring ruler.
summary.zh: 霍克納坡上的芋田中，兩株最秀美的芋並肩而生，互訂終身。酋長點名取其入宴，二芋屢屢遷徙逃避，由科納到懷奧希努，終於振翅飛天；一面有友人告密、一面有友人報信，追逐不休。最後他們在善待他們的酋長治下安家，兒孫繞膝，安享天年——人稱『畏釜芋』。韋斯特維爾特認為此神話或源自古夏威夷臣民改投他酋之權。

passages.text: The old Hawaiians were frequently myth makers; they imagined many a fairy-story for the different localities of the islands. The myth of the two taro plants belongs to South Kona, Hawaii. A chief lived on the mountain-side above Hookena; his people cultivated taro, made kapa cloth, and prepared the trunks of koa-trees for canoes. He had a very fine taro patch, and in one part of the taro pond, side by side, grew two taro plants - finer, stronger, and more beautiful than the others. The leaf stalks bent over in more perfect curves, the leaves developed in graceful proportions, and mutual admiration filled the hearts of the two taro plants, resulting in pledges of undying affection.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 4 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the chief was talking to his servants about the food to be made ready for a feast, and ordered the two especially fine taro plants to be pulled up. A servant came to the home of the two lovers and told them they were to be taken by the chief. Because of their great affection for each other they determined to cling to life as long as possible, and moved to another part of the taro patch. But the chief soon saw them in their new home and again ordered their destruction; again they fled. This happened from time to time until the angry chief determined they should be taken no matter what part of the pond they might be in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 4 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two taro plants took to themselves wings and made a short flight to a neighboring taro patch; a second flight was made to another part of South Kona, and then to still another, until all Kona was interested in the perpetual pursuit and the perpetual escape. At last there was no part of Kona in which they could be concealed: a friend of the angry chief would reveal their hiding-place while one of their own friends gave warning. At last they leaped into the air and flew on and on until utterly weary, falling into a taro patch near Waiohinu; but their chief had ordered the imu, the cooking-place, to be made ready and hastened along on foot, yet their wings moved more swiftly than his feet. Again they lifted themselves into the sky, and favoring winds carried them into the district of Kau, where they found a new home under a kindly chief, settled down and lived many years under the name of Kalo-eke-eke, the Timid Taro, a large family growing up about them and a happy old age blessing their declining days. It is possible this little story may have grown out of the ancient Hawaiian unwritten law which sometimes permitted the subjects of a chief to move away and transfer their allegiance to some neighboring ruler.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 4 (1915); not verbatim.

region.zh: 夏威夷島寇阿木林（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 5, citing David Malo and N. B. Emerson (New York 1915)

summary.en: Canoe-building was a religious matter. The maker reported his fine koa to the canoe priest, who slept before his shrine: a vision of a naked figure meant rotten wood; a well-dressed man or woman promised a good canoe. Pig, cocoanuts, red fish and awa were sacrificed at the tree's root; the priest raised his stone axe and prayed the male and female patrons of canoe-building to listen to the axe; when the tree began to crack all noise was hushed. 'Grant a canoe which shall be swift as a fish in stormy seas' ran the prayer; and if all kept silence but the priest, the canoe was pronounced safe.
summary.zh: 造獨木舟乃宗教之事。匠人向司舟祭司稟報良木；祭司夜宿神龕前祈夢——見裸體者則木朽，見衣冠楚楚者則木佳。啟工時以豬、椰、紅魚與卡瓦酒獻於樹根；祭司舉石斧禱告雌雄舟神：『聽啊，此斧將伐木造舟。』樹將倒時眾人屏息；又誦『願舟如魚，疾行於怒海』之祝。若眾人守靜、唯祭司有聲，新舟即獲吉兆。

sensitivity.note: Ritual record based on David Malo's account (c. 1840) as quoted by Westervelt; paraphrase only.

passages.text: David Malo, a Hawaiian writer of about the year 1840, says the building of a canoe was a religious matter. When a man found a fine koa tree he went to the priest whose province was canoe-making and said, 'I have found a koa-tree, a fine large tree.' On receiving this information the priest went at night to sleep before his shrine. If in his sleep he had a vision of some one standing naked before him, he knew the koa-tree was rotten and would not go up into the woods to cut that tree; if another tree was found and he dreamed of a handsome well-dressed man or woman standing before him, when he awoke he felt sure that the tree would make a good canoe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 5 (1915), quoting David Malo; not verbatim.

passages.text: Preparations were made to go into the mountains and hew the koa into a canoe; they took with them as offerings a pig, cocoanuts, red fish, and awa. Having come to the place they rested for the night, sacrificing these things to the gods. When the time came to cut down the tree the priest would take his stone axe and offer prayer to the male and female deities who were supposed to be the special patrons of canoe building, showing them the axe and saying: 'Listen now to the axe; this is the axe which is to cut down the tree for the canoe.' Malo says: 'When the tree began to crack, ready to fall, they lowered their voices and allowed no one to make a disturbance. When the tree had fallen, the head priest mounted the trunk and called out, Smite with the axe, and hollow the canoe.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 5 (1915), quoting David Malo; not verbatim.

passages.text: Dr. Emerson gives as one of the prayers sometimes used by the priest when passing along the trunk of the tree: 'Grant a canoe which shall be swift as a fish to sail in stormy seas, when the storm tosses on all sides.' After the canoe had been roughly shaped, the ends pointed, the bottom rounded, the people fastened lines to it to haul it down to the beach; the priest again prayed: 'Oh, canoe gods, look you after this canoe. Guard it from stem to stern, until it is placed in the canoe-house.' When completed, pig and fish and fruits were again offered to the gods. Prayers and incantations were part of the ceremony; there was to be no disturbance or noise, or else it would be dangerous for its owner to go out in his new canoe. If all the people except the priest had been quiet, the canoe was pronounced safe; the lashing of the outrigger was of very great solemnity, because the ability to pass through the high surf waves depended so much upon the outrigger as a balance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 5 (1915), quoting Emerson and Malo; not verbatim.

title.en: Laka and the Little People of the Forest

region.zh: 夏威夷群島森林（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 5 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Laka sought through the forests for the best tree and felled it with his stone axe - but on the morrow the log was gone and the forest undisturbed. Twice again he cut, twice again the tree rose by night. Watching at last, he saw in the shadows a host of the little people working with miraculous powers, raising the tree and setting it in its place; he caught the king of the gnomes and learned how to gain their aid instead of their opposition, and by their help his canoe was taken to the shore and fashioned beautifully for wonderful and successful voyages.
summary.zh: 拉卡伐木造舟，翌日木材卻無影無蹤，森林完好如初；再伐再失。他潛伏窺伺，只見夜影中成群的小人施展神力，拔樹歸位。他擒住侏儒之王，學得馭使其族之術；從此借小人之力，木舟被拖至海濱，造得優美精良，航行屢屢得勝。

passages.text: The story of Laka and the fairies is told to illustrate the difficulties surrounding canoe making. Laka desired to make a fine canoe, and sought through the forests for the best tree available. Taking his stone axe he toiled all day until the tree was felled. Then he went home to rest. On the morrow he could not find the log: the trees of the forest had been apparently undisturbed. Again he cut a tree, and once more could not find the log.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 5 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last he cut a tree and watched in the night. Then he saw in the night shadows a host of the little people who toil with miraculous powers to support them. They raised the tree and set it in its place and restored it to its wonted appearance among its fellows. But Laka caught the king of the gnomes and from him learned how to gain the aid rather than the opposition of the little people. By their help his canoe was taken to the shore and fashioned into beautiful shape for wonderful and successful voyages.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 5 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Lau-ka-ieie, the Vine Bride, Weds Kawelona

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 6 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Ku and Hina, accepting Pokahi's sacrifices, leave her a foundling girl named Lau-ka-ieie, leaf of the ieie vine, whose companions are birds and flowers and singing land-shells. She dreams of Kawelona, the first-born of a Kauai chief; the singing shell Pupu-kani-oi is sent to find him, riding the winds of her brother Makani-kau. Birds carry the dreaming youth to Lehua; a cloud-boat brings him over the sea; at Waipio seven shells are blown from the precipice top, and the marriage of the vine-maiden and the sun-set chief is celebrated with shark-gods and leaf-people as guests.
summary.zh: 庫與希娜受波卡希祭祀感動，賜下一女嬰——『伊埃藤之葉』勞卡伊埃；飛鳥百花與會唱歌的陸貝皆是她的侍伴。她夢見考愛島酋長長子卡維羅納，遂遣歌貝普普卡尼奧伊騎著風神兄長馬卡尼考去尋他。飛鳥載著夢中的少年飛往雷胡亞島，白雲成舟渡海而來；懷皮奧谷上，七枚貝殼齊鳴於崖頂——藤女與落日之子的婚禮，由鯊神與草木之族共襄盛舉。

sensitivity.note: Kupua-classification list quoted selectively; romance paraphrased.

passages.text: Then a woman and a man came with an infant; they were the god Ku and Hina his wife. They said to Pokahi and her husband, 'We have accepted your sacrifices and have seen that you are childless, so now we have brought you this child to adopt.' Then they disappeared among the trees of the forest, leaving the child, Lau-ka-ieie, leaf of the ieie vine. She was well cared for and grew up into a beautiful woman without fault or blemish. Her companions and servants were the birds and the flowers. One of her friends made whistles of ti leaves, and blew them; then the Singing Shell and the rainbow-coloured shell were found, and in the night the shells sang, and their voices stole their way into the love of Lau-ka-ieie, so she gently sang with them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Lau-ka-ieie dreamed about Kawelona, the setting of the sun, at Lihue, a fine young man, the first-born of one of the high chiefs of Kauai. She told her kahu all about her dream and the distant island, and it was agreed that the one who had the longest fingers should go to find the man of the dream - this was Pupu-kani-oi, the singing shell. She summoned her brother, Makani-kau, chief of the winds, to waft them away in their wind bodies. They journeyed all around the island of Hawaii and up to Oahu, where the Singing Shell fell in love with a chief and turned from her journey, but Makani-kau went on to Kauai; the dragon women of Heeia and Laiewai tried to catch him, but he was too swift. He leaped on a boat chased by a big shark, jumped into the sea, caught its fins, forced it to flee to shore and made it fast among the rocks as the great shark stone Koa-mano at Haena.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Far up on the hill of Fire-Throwing was a vast number of iiwi birds; Makani-kau saw that they were carrying a fine man - this was the one Lau-ka-ieie desired for her husband; they were the bird guardians of Kawelona. Kawelona had dreamed of a beautiful girl who had visited him again and again, and was prepared to meet Makani-kau. Makani-kau called on the great cloud-gods to send the long white cloud-boat, and it soon appeared; Kawelona entered it with fear and lost sight of the island of Lehua and his bird guardians as he sailed out into the sea. Makani-kau turned their boats to Kahoolawe to visit Ka-moho-alii, the ruler of the sharks, who called his sharks to bring food from all the islands and to guard the travellers on their journey. Makani-kau in his wind body carried the boats swiftly to Waipio; Lau-ka-ieie heard her brother's voice calling her from the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Makani-kau and Kawelona were taken by Hina to the top of Mauna Kea; Poliahu and Lilinoe saw the two fine young men, but Makani-kau passed by to his own wonderful home in the caves of the mountains, resting in the heart of mists and fogs, and placed all his travellers there. Then he went down to the sea and called the sharks of Ka-moho-alii, who appeared in their human bodies in the valley of Waipio, feasting and dancing near the ancient temple of Kahuku-welo-welo, where the wonderful shell Kiha-pu was kept. Makani-kau put seven shells on the top of the precipice and they blew until sweet sounds floated over all the land; thus was the marriage of Lau-ka-ieie and Kawelona celebrated. All the shark people rested, soothed by the music. The kupua people were classified by bodies - leaf bodies, flower bodies, bird bodies, tree bodies, shell bodies, cloud bodies, wind bodies, fish, sharks, sea-mosses, peculiar stones and dangerous places of the pali.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Hiilawe Becomes the Mist of the Falls

region.en: Hiilawe Falls, Waipio Valley, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島懷皮奧谷希伊拉維瀑布

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 6 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Hiilawe, the foundling of Waipio precipices, falls ill and summons Makani-kau and Lau-ka-ieie: bury me where I can always see the eyes of the people, and I will change into a wonderful new body. His malo and leis are laid along the valley sides, becoming trees and vines, and Hina makes him live again. Makani-kau carries the body in thunder and lightning to the brow of the highest precipice, where it becomes a stone; his ghost is made by Hina into a kupua, appearing ever as the misty falls of Waipio looking into the eyes of his people.
summary.zh: 懷皮奧崖壁之子希伊拉維病重，喚風神與藤女近前聽囑：『葬我在能常看見族人眼睛之處，我將化為奇妙新體。』他的纏腰帶與花環被安放於谷側，化作樹木藤蔓；希娜使他復生。馬卡尼考於雷電中捧其遺體葬於最高崖頂，遺體化為巨石；其魂則被希娜化為庫普阿——至今仍作懷皮奧雲霧瀑布，凝望族人。

passages.text: Hiilawe became very ill, and called his brother Makani-kau and his sister Lau-ka-ieie to come near and listen. He told them that he was going to die, and they must bury him where he could always see the eyes of the people, and then he would change his body into a wonderful new body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The beautiful girl took his malo and leis and placed them along the sides of the valley, where they became beautiful trees and vines, and Hina made him live again; so Hiilawe became an aumakua of the waterfalls. Makani-kau took the body in his hands and carried it in the thunder and lightning, burying it on the brow of the highest precipice of the valley. Then his body was changed into a stone, which has been lying there for centuries; but his ghost was made by Hina into a kupua, so that he could always appear as the wonderful misty falls of Waipio, looking into the eyes of his people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: The Shark-god Kauhuhu and the Rainbow Sign
title.zh: 鯊神考胡胡與彩虹之兆

region.en: Anao-puhi cave and Aikanaka harbor, Molokai
region.zh: 摩洛凱島鰻穴與食人港

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 7 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Chief Kupa has the two sons of the priest Kamalo killed for beating his sacred drums. The despairing priest carries a black pig to the eel-cave of the shark-god Kauhuhu; his dragon watchers hide him in a taro-rubbish heap, and when the god smells a man his plea - 'Hear my prayer, then perhaps eat me' - buys mercy. Kauhuhu accepts the pig, orders four hundred black pigs, red fish and white chickens within a tabu fence, and promises to come under a rainbow. The promised cloud crosses from Lanai; the storm sweeps Kupa and his people into the harbor, where sharks feast until the waters run red - Aikanaka, the place for man-eaters.
summary.zh: 酋長庫帕因其子敲擊聖鼓而殺之。祭司卡馬洛背黑豬求助於鯊神考胡胡的鰻穴；龍侍將其藏於芋渣堆中。鯊神嗅出人味，祭司急呼『請聽我禱，再食我不遲』；神感其誠，受其豬，命其備黑豬紅魚白雞各四百，築聖籬以待——屆時彩虹跨谷為兆。烏雲自拉奈島渡海而來，暴雨將庫帕一夥沖入港中；群鯊盛宴，血染港水——此港遂名『食人灣』。

passages.text: The two boys of the priest Kamalo delighted in the glorious revelations of sunrise and sunset tossed over the channel between Molokai and Maui. They were taught many of the secrets of the temple by their father, but were warned that certain things were sacred to the gods and must not be touched. The high chief Kupa had a temple in the valley of the harbor called Aikanaka, with two remarkable drums whose skill in beating could reveal his thoughts to the waiting priests. One day Kupa sailed far away to his favorite fishing-grounds, and meanwhile the boys were tempted to go to his heiau and try the wonderful drums; they hastened along the beach, entered the sacred house, took out his drums and began to beat upon them. When Kupa returned they told him how the boys had beaten upon his sacred drums; he was very angry and ordered his mu, or temple sacrifice seekers, to kill the boys and bring their bodies to the heiau to be placed on the altar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 7 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the priest Kamalo heard of the death of his sons, in bitterness of heart he sought revenge. His own power was not great enough to cope with the high chief, so he sought the aid of the seers and prophets of highest repute throughout Molokai; but they feared Kupa and sent him on from one to another. At last he came to the steep precipice overlooking Kalaupapa and Kalawao, climbed down its sides and found the priest of the shark-god, who refused assistance but directed him to a great cave in the bold cliffs south of Kalawao, named Anao-puhi, the cave of the eel, where dwelt the great shark-god Kauhuhu and his guardians Waka and Mo-o, the great dragons. Kamalo plodded along through the rough lava, bearing a black pig across his shoulders as an offering. The watchmen saw him: 'E, here comes a man, food for the great Mano, fish for Kauhuhu.' But the dragons took pity on him and hid him in the rubbish pile of taro peelings, telling him to watch for eight great surf waves, for the god would come in the last great wave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 7 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The eighth wave reared far above the waters, beat far up into the cave and broke into foam, out of which the shark-god emerged. He took his human form and walked around the cave, crying out as he passed the rubbish heap: 'A man is here. I smell him.' The dragons denied it; the god searched and was turning away when Kamalo's pig squealed; then the giant shark-god leaped to the pile and thrust it apart. Kauhuhu instantly caught Kamalo and lifted him from the rubbish up toward his great mouth. Kamalo spoke quickly as the teeth were coming down upon him: 'E Kauhuhu, listen to me. Hear my prayer. Then perhaps eat me.' The shark-god was astonished and did not bite. 'Well for you that you spoke quickly. Speak.' Then Kamalo told about his sons and their death, and that no one dared avenge him. Pity came to the shark-god; he accepted the offering of the hog and said, 'If you had come for any other purpose I would eat you, but your cause is sacred. I will stand as your kahu, your guardian, and sorely punish the high chief Kupa.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 7 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he told Kamalo to take the priest who had sent him on his shoulders, carry him over the precipices to his own heiau at Kaluaaha, and live with him as a fellow-priest; they were to build a tabu fence around the heiau with sacred tabu staffs of white tapa cloth, collect black pigs, red fish and white chickens by the four hundred, and wait patiently for the coming of Kauhuhu. It was to be a strange coming: on the island Lanai they should see a small cloud, white as snow, increasing until it covers the little island; then that cloud shall cross the channel against the wind and climb the mountains of Molokai until it rests on the highest peaks over the valley where Kupa has his temple. 'At that time a great rainbow will span the valley; I shall be in the care of that rainbow.' The weeks and months passed and still Kamalo waited; at last one day a white cloud appeared, crossed the channel, climbed the mountains and rested at the head of the valley, and the watchers saw the glorious rainbow and knew that Kauhuhu had come according to his word. The storm arose at the head of the valley: the winds struggled into a furious gale, the clouds gathered dark as midnight pierced with terrific lightning, and the rain fell in floods sweeping the hillside down into the valley; down came the torrent upon Kupa's heiau, tearing its walls into fragments and washing Kupa and his people into the harbor, where the shark-god had gathered his people - sharks filled the bay and feasted until the waters ran red and all were destroyed. Hence the legendary name of that little harbor, Aikanaka, the place for man-eaters. When great clouds gather on the mountains and a rainbow spans the valley, look out for furious storms which come suddenly sweeping down the valley; and the storm spread over the adjoining lowlands carrying great destruction, but paused at the tabu staff of Kamalo and rushed on either side of the sacred fence, not daring to touch any one who dwelt therein.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 7 (1915); not verbatim.

region.en: Waipio Valley to Hana and Molokai
region.zh: 懷皮奧谷至哈納與摩洛凱

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 8 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Ka-moho-alii, king of sharks, takes human form to marry the bathing beauty Kalei, charging her to guard the child and never let him taste flesh. Born with a shark-mouth on his back, Nanaue is hidden under a kapa cloak until the men's eating-house breaks the mother's protection; bathers and fishermen begin to disappear in a fierce shark's wake. A workman tears away the cape in the taro patch - 'A shark-man!' - and Nanaue, biting and snapping, escapes as a shark down the river. Driven island to island, he is at last netted, speared, and burned in pieces at Molokai's Puu-mano.
summary.zh: 鯊王卡莫霍阿利化身俊酋娶美人卡萊伊，囑其護子勿使見人、終身勿令食肉。嬰兒納瑙埃背生鯊口，母親以布披長遮；入男子食堂破戒食肉後，海中巨鯊頻頻噬人。墾芋之日，工友扯落其披風，眾呼『鯊人！』；納瑙埃化鯊沿河逃逸，輾轉毛伊、摩洛凱，終被漁人網羅槍棒所制，屍身碎割於普烏鯊丘焚化。

passages.text: Ka-moho-alii was the king of all the sharks which frequent Hawaiian waters. When he chose to appear as a man he was always a chief of dignified, majestic appearance. One day, while swimming back and forth just beneath the surface at the mouth of Waipio Valley, he saw an exceedingly beautiful woman coming to bathe in the white surf. That night he came to the beach black with lava sand, crawled out of the water, and put on the form of a man; as a mighty chief he walked through the valley and mingled with the people, and when he found her he won her to be his wife. When the time came for a child to be born, Ka-moho-alii charged Kalei to keep careful watch of it and guard its body continually from being seen of men, and never allow the child to eat the flesh of any animal; then he disappeared, never permitting Kalei to have the least suspicion that he was the king of the sharks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 8 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the child was born, Kalei gave to him the name Nanaue, and was exceedingly surprised to find an opening in his back; as the child grew to manhood the opening developed into a large shark-mouth in rows of fierce sharp teeth. From infancy to manhood Kalei protected Nanaue by keeping his back covered with a fine kapa cloak. She was full of fear as she saw Nanaue plunge into the water and become a shark, the mouth on his back opening for any kind of prey; but she kept the terrible birthmark a secret hidden in her own heart. For years she prepared for him the common articles of food, always shielding him from the temptation to eat meat; but when he became a man his grandfather took him to the men's eating-house, where his mother could no longer protect him - meats of all varieties were given him in great abundance, yet he always wanted more; his appetite was insatiable.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 8 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: While under his mother's care he had been taken to the pool into which the great Waipio Falls poured, and there bathed, changing himself into a shark to catch the small fish playing around him. As he became a man he avoided his companions in all bathing and fishing; when the people were out in the deep sea, suddenly a fierce shark would appear in their midst, biting and tearing their limbs and dragging them down. Many of the people disappeared secretly, and great terror filled the homes of Waipio. One day, when the high chief had called all the men of the valley to prepare the taro patches, a fellow-workman tore Nanaue's kapa cape from his shoulders; the men behind cried out, 'See the great shark-mouth!' All the people came running together shouting, 'A shark-man!' Nanaue became very angry and snapped his shark-teeth together; he seized one by the arm and bit it in two, tore another's flesh in ragged gashes, and ran biting toward the sea. The crowd surrounded him and he was thrown down and tied; the high chief ordered their largest oven prepared that Nanaue might be burned alive, but during the confusion he changed himself to a shark, the cords fell off, and he rolled into one of the rivers, made a swift rush to the sea and swam away, never again to return to Waipio Valley.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 8 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Apparently Nanaue could not live long in the ocean; he swam over to the island of Maui and landed near the village Hana, dwelling there some time and marrying a chiefess, meanwhile secretly killing and eating some of the people - at last catching a beautiful young girl and carrying her into the deep waters to eat her body in the sight of the people. The Hawaiians launched their canoes and pushed out to kill their enemy, but he swam swiftly away around the island until he landed on Molokai. Again one by one those who went bathing and fishing disappeared. The kahunas of the people heard from their fellow-priests of Maui that there was a dangerous shark-man roaming through the islands, and sent warning urging all trusty fishermen to keep strict watch. At last they saw Nanaue change himself into a great fish; they waged a fierce battle, entangled him in their nets, pierced him with spears and struck him with clubs until the waters were red with his blood, calling on the gods of the sea and uttering prayers and incantations. Nanaue lost strength and could not throw off the ropes nor break the nets; the fishermen drew him to the shore, dragged the great shark body up the hill Puu-mano, cut it into small pieces and burned them in a great oven. Thus died Nanaue, whose cannibal life was best explained by giving to him in mythology the awful appetite of an insatiable man-eating shark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 8 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Kukali's Banana Skin and the Bird-god Halulu
title.zh: 庫卡利的香蕉皮與巨鳥神哈魯魯

region.zh: 遠方之國卡希基（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 9 (New York 1915)

summary.en: A priest's son, Kukali carries a banana whose skin refills forever. Roving to Kahiki, he is snatched by Halulu, a flesh-eating bird-god whose every feather bears talons, and dropped into its walled prison-valley with the bird's other victims. Feeding them from the magic skin and arming them with lava knives, he leads them against the feathers, hacking wing from wing until the screaming god falls into the pit and is burned. Two breast-feathers fly to his sister Namakaeha, of Pele's family, dwelling in a bottomless pit; descending by a broken rope, Kukali falls into a pool of the water of life, conquers the sorcerers, marries the chiefess, and sails home.
summary.zh: 祭司之子庫卡利懷揣神蕉——蕉皮剝而復盈。遠航卡希基，被食人巨鳥神哈魯魯擄入絕谷囚牢。他以神蕉養壯囚伴，授以熔岩石刀，率眾斫其翎、斷其翼，巨鳥慘鳴墜谷，被焚為灰。兩根胸羽飛往其妹納瑪卡埃哈（佩蕾族裔）所居無底之坑；庫卡利繫繩而下，繩斷之際默呼護命咒，落入生命之水而得全；降伏諸巫，娶得女酋，攜眷返鄉。

sensitivity.note: Water-of-life motif links this Hawaiian tale to the quest-immortality cluster.

passages.text: Kukali, according to the folk-lore of Hawaii, was born at Kalapana, the most southerly point of the largest island of the Hawaiian group, hundreds of years ago in the days of the migrations of Polynesians from one group of islands to another. Kukali's father was a priest of great wisdom and ability, who taught his children how to exercise strange and magical powers. To Kukali he gave a banana with the impressive charge to preserve the skin whenever he ate the fruit, and be careful that it was always under his control. He taught Kukali the wisdom of the makers of canoes, how to select fine-grained lava for stone knives and hatchets, the prayers and incantations of greatest efficacy, and charms which would be more powerful than any charms his enemies might use. Kukali went inland through the forests carrying no food save the banana; hunger came, and he carefully stripped back the skin and ate the banana, folding the skin once more together. In a little while the skin was filled with fruit; again and again he ate, and the fruit always again filled the skin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 9 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: With prayers he fashioned a great canoe and sailed on and on, guided by the sun in the day and the stars in the night, until he came to the strange lands of Kahiki. A great bird which lived on human flesh was the god of the land; its name was Halulu, and each feather of its wings was provided with talons and seemed to be endowed with human powers. Over its deep valley, walled in like the valley of the Arabian Nights, the great bird hovered looking into the depths for food; a strong wind always attended the coming of Halulu when he sought the valley for his victims. Kukali was lifted on the wings of the bird-god and carried to this hole and quietly laid on the ground to finish his hour of deep sleep. When he awoke he found himself in the shut-in valley with many companions captured by the great bird, weak and dying, while Halulu perched on a tree on the edge of the precipice and let down its wing to sweep across the floor of the valley and pick up its victims.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 9 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kukali pitied the helpless state of his fellow-prisoners and prepared his best incantations and prayers. He took his wonderful banana and fed all the people until they were very strong; he taught them how to seek stones best fitted for the manufacture of knives and hatchets, and for days they worked until they were all well armed with sharp stone weapons. While they made preparation for the final struggle the bird-god had often come to his perch and put his wing down into the valley; at last he became impatient and sent his strongest feathers along the precipitous walls seeking for victims. Kukali and his companions ran out from their hiding-places and fought the strong feathers, cutting them off and chopping them into small pieces; Halulu cried out with pain and anger, and sent feather after feather into the prison, until one wing was entirely destroyed and then the other was broken to pieces. The bird-god put down a strong leg armed with great talons; after a fierce battle they cut off the leg and destroyed the talons, and hacked and pulled until the bird-god, screaming with pain, fell into the pit among the prisoners, who quickly cut the body into fragments. The prisoners made steps in the walls, climbed out by aid of vines, gathered great piles of branches, threw them in until the body was covered, and burned Halulu to ashes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 9 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: But two of the breast feathers of the burning Halulu flew away to his sister, who lived in a great hole which had no bottom; the name of this sister was Namakaeha, and she belonged to the family of Pele, the goddess of volcanic fires, who had journeyed to Hawaii and taken up her home in the crater of Kilauea. Namakaeha smelled smoke on the feathers and knew her brother was dead. Kukali came to the great pit; a rope of hau tree bark was fastened around his body, and he went down and down until, owing to counter incantations of Namakaeha's priests, the rope broke and he fell. Remembering the prayer which a falling man must use, he cried, 'O Ku! guard my life!' - and his incantation threw him into a pool of the water of life and he was saved. One of the kahunas caring for Namakaeha warned him against eating anything that was ripe, because it would be poison; but Kukali had carefully preserved his wonderful banana skin and was able to eat apparently ripe fruit and yet be perfectly safe. The kahunas tried to overcome him and destroy him, but he conquered them, killed those who were bad and entered into friendship with those who were good; he accepted the fruits offered him but always ate the food in his magic banana, conquered even the chiefess and married her, and at last persuaded her, as her relative Pele had already done, to sail away with their family in a large canoe to Hawaii, their future home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 9 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: The Rainbow-maiden and the Test of Ghosts

region.zh: 瓦胡島馬諾阿谷與威基基

texts.period: Hawaiian oral tradition (Kalakaua family version); retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 11 (New York 1915)

summary.en: The shark-blooded chief Kauhi repeatedly murders the rainbow-maiden Kahalaopuna; the owl-god Pueo digs her up alive until she is buried beneath a koa's roots. Her spirit drifts to Mahana, who finds and restores her with his witch-doctor brother and two guardian spirit-sisters. To prove her alive before the king, Mahana wagers Kauhi into the ovens; Kauhi's sorcerers lay ape leaves for the girl to walk on, since ghosts leave no torn footprints - but Kahala, coached by the spirits, breaks them herself, and the sorcerer who leans over the water-calabash to catch ghost-faces has his own spirit face crushed by the mountain-god Akaaka.
summary.zh: 鯊族酋長考希屢殺彩虹少女卡哈拉歐普納；貓頭鷹神普埃奧屢掘屍復生，直到少女被深埋於寇阿樹根之下。其魂飄至瑪哈納處；他與兄長巫醫及兩位守護精靈姐妹合力救活了她。為在君王面前證明她尚在人間，瑪哈納與考希賭命：若姑娘現身，考希自願入烤爐。考希的巫師們鋪下芋葉——鬼魂行過不會踏破葉片；精靈姐妹教少女親手踏碎蕉芋之葉；而俯身水盆捕捉鬼影的巫師，其自家魂影被山神阿卡阿卡一把捏碎，當場斃命。

sensitivity.note: Ghost-test record: ape-leaf and water-reflection tests as Hawaiian forensic belief.

passages.text: The natives of Manoa Valley usually give the rainbow-maiden the name of Kahalaopuna, the Hala of Puna; sometimes they call her Kaikawahine Anuenue, the Rainbow Maiden. The legend says that the rainbow-maiden had two lovers, one from Waikiki and one from Kamoiliili; both wanted the beautiful arch to rest over their homes and the maiden, the descendant of the gods, to dwell therein. Kauhi, the Waikiki chief, was of the family of Mohoalii, the shark-god, and partook of the shark's cruel nature. He became angry with the rainbow-maiden and killed her and buried the body, but her guardian god, Pueo, the owl, scratched away the earth and brought her to life. Several times this occurred, and the owl each time restored the buried body to the wandering spirit; at last the chief buried the body deep down under the roots of a large koa-tree. The owl-god scratched and pulled, but the roots of the tree were many and strong; his claws were entangled again and again, and at last he concluded that life must be extinct and deserted the place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 11 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The spirit of the murdered girl was wandering around hoping it could be restored to the body and not be compelled to descend to Milu, the Under-world; the shadows of real death were encompassing her. At last she saw a noble young chief approaching - Mahana, the chief of Kamoiliili. The spirit hovered over him and tried to impress her anguish upon him; he felt the call of distress and attributed it to a ghost or aumakua, a ghost-god, and was conscious of an influence leading him toward a large koa-tree. There he found the earth disturbed by the owl-god, tore aside the roots and discovered the body bruised and disfigured, yet recognized it as the body of the rainbow-maiden whom he had loved. Mahana's elder brother was a kahuna of great celebrity, called at once to pronounce the prayers and invocations necessary for influencing the spirit and the body to reunite; in his anxiety he called upon the spirits of two sisters who as aumakuas watched over the welfare of Mahana's clan. These spirit-sisters brought the spirit of the rainbow-maiden to the bruised body and induced it to enter the feet; then, while the kahuna chanted and used his charms, they pushed the spirit of Kahala slowly up the body until the soul was once more restored to its beautiful tenement.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 11 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mahana determined to provoke Kauhi, and by the skilful use of Kahala's story led him to admit that he had killed the rainbow-maiden and buried her body. Mahana said that Kahala was now alive and visiting his sisters. Kauhi was so sure that Kahala was dead that he offered to be baked alive in one of the native imus if she should be produced before the king and the principal chiefs; Akaaka, the grandfather of Kahala, one of the mountain-gods of Manoa Valley, was to be one of the judges. Kauhi feared deception and consulted the sorcerers of his own family: it was necessary to be prepared to test the ghosts, for if ghosts were present the aid of spirit catchers from the land of Milu could be invoked to seize the venturesome ghosts and carry them away for punishment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 11 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chief sorcerer of Kauhi's family told him to take the large and delicate leaves of the ape-plant and spread them over the place where Kahala must walk and sit before the judges; a human being could not touch these leaves without tearing and bruising them, but a ghost walking upon them could make no impression. Untorn leaves would condemn Mahana to the ovens, and the spirit catchers would seize the escaped ghost. The leaves were secretly placed; Kahala drew near, attended by the two spirit-sisters who had saved her, and they knew at once the ghost test by which she was to be tried: the test would only prove more evidently that she was a living human being, but would prove that they themselves were ghosts. They whispered to her to break as many of the leaves on either side of her as she could without attracting undue attention, and Kahala bruised and broke as many of the leaves as she could quietly. She was recognized at once as the child of the divine rain and wind of Manoa Valley; the torn leaves afforded ample and indisputable testimony, and Kauhi in despair recognized the girl whom he had several times tried to slay. A second form of ghost-testing was proposed by Akaaka: any face reflected in a pool or calabash of water was a spirit face, which the watcher grasped and crushed, destroying the spirit. The chief sorcerer eagerly ordered a calabash of water brought; in his anxiety he forgot himself and leaned over the calabash. His own spirit face was the only one reflected on the surface; before he could leap back and restore his spirit to his body, Akaaka leaped forward, thrust his hands down into the water and seized and crushed this spirit face between his mighty hands. The chief sorcerer fell dead by the side of the calabash by means of which he had hoped to destroy the friends of the rainbow-maiden. Kauhi was punished for his crimes: he was baked alive in the imu prepared on his own land at Waikiki, and his lands and retainers were given to Kahala and Mahana.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 11 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: How Milu Became King of the Ghosts

region.en: Waipio Valley, Hawaii Island, and Po (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 夏威夷島懷皮奧谷與幽冥（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 12 (New York 1915)

summary.en: The healing god Kamaka spits into the mouth of the red-skinned farmer Lono and makes him the father of Hawaiian medicine. Milu, chief of Waipio, is healed by Lono but warned to dwell quietly in a ti-leaf house and never look out. A giant bird tears out his liver when he peeps; Lono restores him with the wrapped blood. Warned again, Milu goes surf-riding, and two returning waves crush him under. Lono remains the ancestor of good healing priests, but Milu becomes ruler of the Under-world, where ghosts surf, gamble, box and feast as they did in life.
summary.zh: 治病之神卡馬卡向紅膚農夫龍諾口中吐唾，使其成為夏威夷醫術之祖。懷皮奧酋長米盧得龍諾救治，卻被告誡：幽居芋葉小屋、切莫窺探窗外。一日巨鳥撲落，撕取其肝；龍諾以布裹血敷創救之。再被告誡後，米盧仍忍不住出海弄潮——兩道回擊的巨浪將他捲入海底。龍諾成為良醫之祖，米盧則成幽冥之王：鬼魂在其治下衝浪、博弈、角力、宴飲，一如生前。

sensitivity.note: Under-world cosmology: Milu vs. New Zealand Miru noted by Westervelt.

passages.text: Lono was a chief living on the western side of the island Hawaii. He had a very red skin and strange-looking eyes; his choice of occupation was farming, and this man had never been sick. One time he was digging with the oo, a long sharp-pointed stick or spade, and cut his foot; a stranger, Kamaka, a god of healing, was sent for and bound pounded popolo fruit and leaves with salt upon the wound. As he journeyed on, Lono followed, saying he had left his lands in the care of friends and hastened after him to learn how to heal other people. The god said, 'Lono, open your mouth!' This Lono did, and the god spat in his mouth, so that the saliva could be taken into every part of Lono's body; thus a part of the god became a part of Lono, and he became very skilful in the use of all healing remedies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The god said, 'It is not right for us to stay together; you must go to a separate place and give yourself up to healing people.' Lono turned aside to dwell in Waimanu and Waipio Valleys and began to practise healing, becoming very noted. Another god, Kalae, was trying to find some way to kill Milu, chief of Waipio, and was always making him sick; Milu heard of the skill of Lono, who came, slapped Milu all over the body and healed him from all the sickness inside the body caused by Kalae. But there was danger from outside, so he said: 'You must build a ti-leaf house and dwell there quietly for some time, letting your disease rest. If a company should come by the house making sport with a great noise, do not go out, because when you go they will come up and get you for your death. Do not open the ti leaves and look out; the day you do this you shall die.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: For some time Milu remained in the house; then Waipio was full of resounding noises and a great bird appeared in the sky, resplendent in all kinds of feathers, swaying from precipice to precipice, while the people shouted until the valley re-echoed. Milu became tired of that great noise and could not patiently obey his physician, so he pushed aside some of the ti leaves of his house and looked out upon the bird. That was the time when the bird swept down upon the house, thrusting a claw under Milu's arm and tearing out his liver. Lono saw this and ran after the bird, which flew to a deep pit in the lava and dashed inside, leaving blood spread on the stones; Lono came, saw the blood, took it and wrapped it in a piece of tapa cloth and returned to the place where the chief lay almost dead. He poured some medicine into the wound and pushed the tapa and blood inside, and Milu was soon healed. The place where the bird hid is called to this day Ke-ake-o-Milu, the liver of Milu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Lono told him that another death threatened him and would soon appear; he must dwell in quietness. For some time Milu lived in peace; then one day the surf of Waipio became very high and the people entered into surf-riding with great joy and loud shouts. Milu was impatient of the restraint and forgot the words of Lono, and went out to bathe in the surf. He let the first and second waves go by and launched himself upon the third; he went out again, and as he came to the shore the first and second waves were hurled back from the shore in a great mass against the wave upon which he was riding; the two great masses of water struck and pounded Milu, whirling and crowding him down, while the surf-board was caught in the raging waters and thrown toward the shore. Milu was completely lost in the deep water. The people cried, 'Milu is dead! The chief is dead!' The god Kalae thought he had killed Milu, so he with the other poison-gods went on a journey to Mauna Loa, where Kapo and Pua, the poison-gods of Maui, joined them; they discovered a forest on Molokai and entered into the trees of that forest as kupua spirits, becoming the medicinal or poison qualities in the trees. Lono remained in Waipio Valley, becoming the ancestor and teacher of all the good healing priests of Hawaii, but Milu became the ruler of the Under-world, where he established ghostly sports like those his subjects had enjoyed before death - kilu with polished cocoanut shells, konane, gambling, boxing and wrestling, leaping from precipices into ghostly swimming-pools, feasting and fighting - living the ghost life as they had on earth. Sometimes the ruler was forgotten and the ancient Hawaiians called the Under-world by his name, Milu; the New Zealanders frequently gave their Under-world the name Miru.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Ka-ilio-hae Visits the King of Ghosts

region.en: Kekaa, Lahaina, Maui, and the ghost-land (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 毛伊島拉海納凱卡與幽冥（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 13 (New York 1915)

summary.en: The wild dog Ka-ilio-hae sinks into death; his spirit creeps from the left eye, perches like a bird, and is borne toward Kekaa, doorway of Maui's ghosts. His ghost-sister, an aumakua-ho-ola, warns him never to taste the shadow-food, and coaches him through the three watchmen and the two blocking heads to the court of the ghost king Walia: answer 'Walia' and 'The Great Death', push the heads aside, and cry 'He comes to see the Divine One'. Before the third call seals the walls, she drives him home and shoves the shivering spirit back into the foot, up the body, to life.
summary.zh: 『野狗』卡伊利奧哈埃沉入彌留；魂魄自左眼竄出，如鳥棲枝，被引往毛伊鬼魂之門凱卡。其幽魂姐姐——能起死回生的奧馬庫阿——告誡他勿食幻影之食，並傳授過三關、避雙頭、朝見鬼王瓦利亞的口訣。第三聲召喚將封閉石牆之前，姐姐硬將他拖回海濱；亡魂畏懼軀體的氣味屢屢逃縮，被姐姐自腳踝推入、順體而上——胸口起伏，家人知道他又活過來了。

passages.text: When any person lay in an unconscious state it was supposed by the ancient Hawaiians that death had taken possession of the body and opened the door for the spirit to depart. Ka-ilio-hae, the wild dog, had been sick for days and at last sank into unconsciousness. The spirit of life crept out of the body and finally departed from the left eye into a corner of the house, buzzing like an insect; it looked back over the body it had left, which appeared like a massive mountain with eyes like deep caves. The spirit became afraid, went outside and rested on the roof of the house; the people began to wail loudly, and the ghost fled from the noise to a cocoanut-tree and perched like a bird in the branches. Soon he felt the impulse of the spirit-land moving him away from his old home; he leaped from tree to tree and flew from place to place, wandering toward Kekaa, the place from which the ghosts leave the island of Maui for their home in the permanent spirit-land, the Under-world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 13 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Near this doorway to the spirit-world he met the ghost of a sister who had died long before, to whom was given the power of sometimes turning a ghost back to its body again - an aumakua-ho-ola, a spirit making alive. She called to him and warned him that when her husband was at home he must not yield to any invitation from him to enter their house nor partake of any of the food her husband might urge him to eat: the home and the food would be only the shadows of real things, and would destroy his power of becoming alive again. She led him to the place of whirlwinds where many spirits were planning to enjoy all the sports of their former life - surf-riding, rolling the ulu-maika, boxing, wrestling, gambling games, and crowds around the hulas. There was a strange quality which fettered every new-born ghost: he could only go in the direction into which he was pushed by the hand of some stronger power; the newcomer started to join the games, but the sister slapped him on the breast and drove him away, for these were shadow games into which those who entered could never go back to the substantial things of life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 13 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the sister led her brother to a great field, stone walled, in which were such fine grass houses as were built only for chiefs of the highest rank, and pointed to a narrow passage into which he must enter by himself. 'This is the home of Walia, the high chief of the ghosts living in this place. You must go to him. Listen to all he says to you. Say little. Return quickly. There will be three watchmen guarding this passage. The first will ask you, What is the fruit of your heart? You will answer, Walia. The second watchman will ask why you come; again answer, Walia. At the end of the entrance the third guardian stands holding a raised spear ready to strike; call to him, Ka-make-loa, the Great Death - that is the name of his spear - then reply, To see the chief. When you stand at the door of the great house you will see two heads bending together so that you cannot enter; point your hands straight before you between them and open your arms, pushing these guards off on each side, then the ala-nui, the great way, will be open for you. You will see kahilis moving over the chiefs; the king will awake and call, Why does this traveller come? You will reply quickly, He comes to see the Divine One. Listen and remember and you will be alive again.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 13 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ka-ilio-hae did as he was told with the three watchmen, and each one stepped back, saying 'Noa' - the tabu is lifted - and he pushed by. At the door he shoved the two heads to the side and entered the chief's house, falling on his hands and knees while the servants waved the kahilis. The chief awoke, looked at him and said: 'Aloha, stranger, come near. Who is the high chief of your land?' Then Ka-ilio-hae gave the name of his king and the genealogy from ancient times of the chiefs dead and in the spirit-world. The queen of ghosts arose, and the kneeling spirit saw one more beautiful than any woman in all the island, and fell on his face before her. The king told him to go back and enter his body and tell his people about troubles near at hand. While he was before the king twice he heard messengers call that the sports were all over; any one not heeding would be thrown into the darkest place of the home of the ghosts when the third call had been sounded. The sister knew that at the third call the stone walls around the king's houses would close and her brother would be held fast forever in the spirit-land; she uttered her incantations, passed the guard, softly called, seized him and pushed him outside. She knew well what must be done to restore the spirit to the body; when they came to the place where the body lay she found a hole in the corner of the house and pushed the spirit through. When he saw the body he was very much afraid and tried to escape, but the sister caught him and pushed him inside the foot up to the knee; he did not like the smell of the body and tried to rush back, but she pushed him inside again and held the foot fast and shook him and made him go to the head. The family heard a little sound in the mouth and saw breath moving the breast, then they knew that he was alive again; they warmed the body and gave a little food, and when strength returned he told his family all about his wonderful journey into the land of ghosts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 13 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Kalai-pahoa, the Poison-god of the Trees

region.zh: 摩洛凱島冒納羅亞林（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 14 (New York 1915)

summary.en: After Milu's death the death-gods left Waipio for Maui and entered the trees of a Mauna Loa forest, becoming the medicine and poison of the woods. The ruined gambler Kane-ia-kama, told in dream to 'bet your bones', wins everything and is shown which trees hold the gods; offerings set, he sends woodcutters whose sap-blood and flying chips kill them - until leaf cloaks of ieie protect the men. The chief cuts the gods from their trees; the strongest, named Kalai-pahoa, killed all who drank at a poisoned spring, passed from Kahekili to Kamehameha, and lies in the Bishop Museum today.
summary.zh: 米盧死後，諸死神自懷皮奧遷往毛伊，遁入冒納羅亞林中諸樹，化為草木之藥性與毒性。傾家賭徒卡內亞卡馬夜聞神諭『以骨為注』，連戰連勝，又被指認諸神所棲之樹。他遣人伐木取神：樹血飛濺，伐木者暴斃；以伊埃藤葉為衣方得安然。最強之神名『卡萊帕霍亞』——意為『被石斧所刻者』——其毒泉曾使飲者全滅；後由毛伊王卡赫基利傳至卡美哈梅哈，今藏於檀香山主教博物館。

sensitivity.note: Poison-rite (pule-ana-ana) summarized; no operational detail beyond the legend's own terms.

passages.text: The Bishop Museum of Honolulu has images of many of the gods of long ago: a helmeted head of wicker-work covered with red feathers bordered with yellow - the mighty war-god of Kamehameha - and a squat rough image crudely carved out of wood, Kamehameha's poison-god. The ancient Hawaiians were acquainted with poisons of various kinds; one Hawaiian writer said: 'The opihi-awa is a poison shell-fish, bitter and deadly; Kalai-pahoa is also a tree in which there is the power to kill.' Kamehameha's poison-god was called Kalai-pahoa because it was cut from that tree which grew in the upland forest on the island of Molokai.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 14 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the priest wanted Kalai-pahoa he was taken down and anointed with cocoanut-oil and wrapped in a fresh kapa cloth, set up above the altar with a feast before him - awa to drink, and pig, fish, and poi to eat. The priest who had special care of this god would scrape off a little from the wood, put it in an awa cup, hold the cup before the god, chanting a prayer for the life of the king, the government and the people; one of the priests would drink the contents and quickly take food. Those watching would see a red flush creep over his cheeks while the eyes became glassy and the breath short like that of a dying man; then the priest would touch his lips to the stick Mai-ola and have his life restored - Mai-ola was a god who had another tree, and when Kalai-pahoa entered his tree on Molokai, Mai-ola entered another tree and became the enemy of the poison-god. The priests of the poison-god were powerful in the rite called pule-ana-ana, praying to death: it was believed they scraped the body of the image and put the pieces in the food of the one they wished to pray to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 14 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: A legend told by the old people explained the coming of medicinal and poisonous properties into the trees. After the death of Milu the gods left Waipio Valley and crossed the channel to Maui; these gods had all kinds of power for evil - stopping the breath, chilling or burning the body, inflicting death. Pua and Kapo, goddesses having medicinal power, joined the party, and all the gods went up Mauna Loa into a large and magnificent forest which they loved and of which they became gods. Near this forest lived Kane-ia-kama, a high chief who was a very great gambler and had gambled away all his possessions; in sleep he heard a voice, 'O Kane-ia-kama, begin your play again', and when he protested he had nothing left, the voice said, 'Bet your bones, and see what will happen.' He bet his body and won until he had more wealth than any one on the island.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 14 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the voice showed him the trees into which the gods had entered, explained all their characteristics, and ordered him to take offerings of pigs, fish, cocoanuts, bananas, chickens and kapas and place them at the roots of these trees. For some reason he sent woodcutters to cut the gods out of them with their stone axes. They began to cut: the koko, the blood of the trees as the natives termed the flowing sap, and the chips flying out struck some of the woodcutters and they fell dead. Kane-ia-kama made cloaks of the long leaves of the ieie vine and tied them around his men so that their bodies could not be touched, then the work was easily accomplished. The chief kept these images of gods cut from the medicinal trees; the most powerful was that whose voice he had heard in the night, to which he gave the name Kalai-pahoa, The-one-cut-by-the-stone-axe. It was said that when Kane-kulana-ula changed into his tree form he leaped into it with a tremendous flash of lightning, thus the great mana went into that tree. A piece of this tree fell into a spring at Kaakee near the maika field on Molokai, and all the people who drank at that spring died; they filled it up, and the chiefs ruled that no one should keep branches or pieces of the tree - only the carved gods were to be preserved. Kahekili, king of Maui, had these images as household gods and told Kamehameha to wait and he should have the poison-god and the government over all the islands; after Kahekili's death Kamehameha did conquer all the islands and Kalai-pahoa came into his possession. The overthrow of idolatry came in 1819, when most of the wooden gods were burned or thrown into ponds and rivers, but a few were concealed by their caretakers, among them the two gods now in the Bishop Museum.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 14 (1915); not verbatim.

region.zh: 摩洛凱至基拉韋厄（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 16 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Out surfing, chief Puna is lured to Molokai by Kiha-wahine, who keeps him in a cave-house as husband. Her brother Hinole recognizes him and coaches his escape: ask for the ice-water of Poliahu, and bore a hole in the jar. The dragon goes for the water, finds it leaking on the ground, and Puna has reached Pele's pit. Gathering all the dragons of the islands, she threatens to fill the crater; they spit drool that almost quenches the fire - but the flames rise, burn the dragons, and Kiha-wahine leaps into the shadow-lake Loko-aka. Her brother Hinole becomes the hinalea fish; Puna returns to Haumea, and is later hanged in a breadfruit tree by chief Kou - the tree opens and swallows his wife, whose akala skirt still grows as a vine.
summary.zh: 衝浪之時，酋長普納被龍女基哈瓦希內誘至摩洛凱，囚於洞屋為夫。其兄希諾勒認出他並授計逃脫：求取冒納凱阿雪山之冰水，並在水罐上鑽孔。龍女負罐遠行，發現罐水漏盡，普納已抵佩蕾火山口。她召來群島之龍圍攻火山口，口吐涎沫幾滅神火；火勢驟起，燒斃群龍，龍女跳入影湖羅科阿卡。其兄希諾勒化為海鏢鱸魚；普納返歸妻室，後被酋長庫縊於麵包樹——樹身裂開吞入其妻，其紅藤裙至今仍生為藤蔓。

sensitivity.note: Dragon (mo-o) cycle; Westervelt notes this is a reworking of 'The Wonderful Breadfruit Tree'.

passages.text: Haumea is said to have taken as her husband Puna, a chief of Oahu. He and his people were going around the island; the surf was not very good and they wanted to find a better place. At last they found a fine surf-place where a beautiful woman was floating on the sea. She called to Puna, 'This is not a good place for surf'; he asked where there was one, and she answered, 'I know where there is one, far outside.' She desired to get Puna; they swam way out in the sea until they were out of sight, and forgot everything else but each other. This woman was Kiha-wahine. The people on the beach wailed but did not take canoes to help them; they swam over to Molokai, left their surf-boards on the beach and went inland to the cave house of the woman. Puna stayed there as a kind of prisoner and obeyed her commands; she took care of him and prepared his food, and they lived as husband and wife for a long time, until at last his real body began to change.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 16 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Once he went out of the cave and heard voices loud and confused, but could not go, because the woman had laid her law on him that if he went away he would be killed. In the morning he went down to the sea and saw many sports; while he was watching, one of the men, Hinole, the brother of his wife, saw him and was pleased, inviting him to eat and talk. Hinole asked whence he came; Puna told him all the story, and Hinole told him his wife was a goddess: 'When you return and come near to the place, go very easily and softly, and you will see her in her real nature as a mo-o, or dragon; but she knows all that you are doing and what we are saying. Your first wife, Haumea, is the first born of all the other women. It is my thought to save your life, so that you can look into the eyes of your first wife.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 16 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Puna went slowly and softly back and saw his wife as a dragon; she heard his breathing, quickly changed to a human body and cursed him for coming quietly and hiding, saying, 'Perhaps I will eat your eyes.' But they dwelt together and had peace. One day Puna was breathing hard, for he was thirsty and wanted the water of the gods - the water of Poliahu of Mauna Kea, the snow-covered mountain of Hawaii, cold and heavy with ice, which his good grandparents always brought for him in his youth. The woman said, 'Your desire for water is not a hard thing to satisfy; I will go and get the water.' Before he had spoken of his desire he had made a little hole in the water-jar, as Hinole had told him, that the woman might spend a long time and let him escape. She arose and went away; he also arose and followed, found a canoe and crossed to Maui, another boat going to Hawaii, and landed at Kau. He went up and stood on the edge of the pit of Pele; those living in the crater saw him and cried out, 'Here is a man, a husband for our sister.' He quickly went down into the crater and dwelt with them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 16 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kiha-wahine went to Poliahu, but could not fill the water-jar: when the jar was lifted it became light, and she saw the water lying on the ground and her husband far beyond at the pit of Pele. She became angry and called all the dragons of Molokai, Lanai, Maui, Kahoolawe and Hawaii; when she had gathered them she went up to Kilauea and stood on the edge of the crater, telling the people below to give her the husband.
