They refused, crying out, 'Where is your husband? This is the husband of our sister; he does not belong to you, O mischief-maker.' Then the dragon-goddess said, 'If you do not give up this man, I will send all my people and fill up this crater and capture all your fires.' The dragons threw their drooling saliva in the pit and almost destroyed the fire where Pele lived; then the fire moved and began to rise with great strength, burning off all the saliva, and Kiha-wahine and the rest of the dragons could not stand the heat; the fire caught them and killed a large part, while earthquakes opened the rocks and fire followed the fleeing dragons. Kiha-wahine ran and leaped down the precipice into a fish-pond called by the name of the shadow of the dragon, Loko-aka, the shadow lake; so she was imprisoned in the pond, husbandless, scarcely escaping with her life. When she went back to Molokai she meant to kill Hinole for aiding Puna to escape, but he leaped into the sea and became the Hinalea, a fish dearly loved by the fishermen of the islands; she caught him at last in a basket baited with pounded sea-eggs and crabs - this is the way the Hinalea is caught to this day - and compelled him ever after to retain the form of the fish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 16 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: After Puna had escaped according to the directions of Hinole he returned to Oahu and saw his wife Haumea. After Puna disappeared, Kou became the new chief of Oahu, and Puna went to live in the mountains above Kalihi-uka. One day he came to a banana plantation, ate, and lay down to rest; the watchmen of the new chief found him, took his loin-cloth, tied his hands behind his back, and brought him to Kou, who killed him and hung the body in the branches of a breadfruit-tree at Wai-kaha-lulu below the steep diving rocks of the Nuuanu stream. When Haumea returned from gathering moss and fish she heard of the death of her husband; as she hurried down all the people shouted, 'This is the wife of the dead man.' She found Puna hanging on the branches; then she made that breadfruit-tree open. Leaving her pa-u on the ground where she stood, she stepped inside the tree and bade it close about her and appear the same as before; the akala of which the pa-u had been made took root and grew into a large vine. The fat of the body of Puna fell down through the branches and the dogs ate below the tree; one of these dogs belonged to the chief Kou: it came back to the house, played with the chief, then leaped, caught him by the throat and killed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 16 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Hiku Swings His Bride Up from Milu

region.en: Waipio pit of Milu, Hawaii Island (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 夏威夷島懷皮奧米盧之坑（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Hawaiian oral tradition (Kalakaua family version); retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology), ch. 18 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Ku's children Hiku and Kewalu wed by the tabu surf of Kona. Hiku pines for the upland forest and slips away through fog, vines and rain; Kewalu, entangled in the ieie she chased him through, winds the vines about her neck - the first suicide in Hawaiian story - and her spirit creeps down to Milu. Ku teaches Hiku the one daring remedy: rub himself with rancid kukui oil, descend by an ieie rope through the Waipio pit, and win the ghost unnoticed. Among the ghosts he wins a kilu game, answers Kewalu's mele with the secret response, swings her in his lap and shrinks her spirit smaller and smaller until Ku hauls them up; sealed in a cocoanut shell, her ghost is poured in at the feet and charmed upward until the eyes open.
summary.zh: 庫神之子女希庫與凱瓦魯在科納聖灘結為夫婦。希庫思慕山林，趁夜遁走；凱瓦魯追夫不成，被伊埃藤纏頸自縊——夏威夷神話中第一宗自殺——其魂徐徐墮入幽冥米盧。庫授奇策：以腐臭寇阿油塗身，循懷皮奧之坑沿伊埃藤而下。冥界中他贏得基盧賭局，以密語應和她之歌；鞦韆戲中攬其入懷，一邊搖盪一邊誦咒使她越縮越小，直至父親收繩上提。魂被封入椰殼，自足底灌入遺體，誦咒引魂上行——雙目終於重開。

sensitivity.note: Descent-resurrection cluster flagship; Westervelt links it to the Maori 'Deceiving of Kewa' chant.

passages.text: Ku, one of the most widely known gods of the Pacific Ocean, was thought by the Hawaiians to have dwelt as a mortal for some time on the western side of the island Hawaii. He chose a chiefess by the name of Hina as his wife, and to them were born two children. When he withdrew from his residence among men he left a son on the uplands of North Kona, and a daughter on the seashore of the same district. The son, Hiku-i-kana-hele, Hiku of the forest, lived with his mother; the daughter, Kewalu, dwelt under the care of guardian chiefs and priests by a temple, and was perfected in all arts pertaining to the very high chiefs. Hiku was proficient in all the feats of manly strength and skill upon which chiefs of the highest rank prided themselves; to him were given many of the supernatural powers of his father, though his mother guarded him from the knowledge that he had a sister.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Day after day the young chief heard the rejoicing of people by the sea; a trusty retainer reported that he had found certain tabu surf waters of the Kona beach where a very high chiefess alone played with her surf-board, her beauty and skill so great that the people clapped their hands like many thunder-storms. Hiku prepared the best surf-board that could be made, anointed his body with kukui oil until it glistened like polished leaves, and went boldly to the tabu surf waters of his sister. The gods of the sea favored Hiku: he carried the surf-board more royally than any chief the people had ever known, and rode to the shore on the crests of the highest waves performing wonderful feats by his magic power. Kewalu took the wreath of rare and fragrant flowers which she wore and threw it around his shoulders as a token to all the people that she had taken him to be her husband; thus Hiku married his sister, Kewalu, according to the custom of that time, because she was the only one of all the people equal to him in rank and beauty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hiku at last grew weary of the life by the sea and wanted the forest on the mountain and the cold air of the uplands. One night he rose up very quietly and passed out into the darkness; the leaves rustled in welcome and the night birds hastened him on, but Kewalu was awakened and hastened after him, her plaintive cry louder and clearer than the voices of the night birds: 'E Hiku, return! O my love, wait for Kewalu!' Hiku by his magic power sent thick fogs and mists around her, threw the long flexible vines of the ieie down into the path, so that she stumbled and fell again and again; the rain destroyed the kapa mantle she had thrown around her. The ancient chant says: Hiku is climbing up the hill; branches and vines are in the way; hopeless the quest, but Kewalu is calling, E Hiku, beloved! At last she could no longer hear the retreating footsteps; chilled and desolate she crept back to the village and into the grass house, intending to put an end to her life. The ieie vines held her arms and legs, but she partially disentangled herself and wound them around her head and neck; soon the tendrils grew tight and slowly but surely choked the beautiful chiefess to death - this was the first suicide in the records of Hawaiian mythology. As the body became lifeless the spirit crept upward to the lua-uhane, the little hole in the corner of the eye, the spirit-door, and slowly and sadly journeyed to Milu, the Under-world home of the ghosts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: His father, the god Ku, had been watching him and had seen the suicide of the beautiful Kewalu. He called Hiku and told him how heedless he had been in his treatment of Kewalu, and that only by the most daring effort could he hope to regain his loved bride: he could go to the Under-world, meet the ghosts and bring his sister back, but if the ghosts discovered and captured him they would punish him with the severest torments. Hiku was determined. He prepared a cocoanut-shell full of oil made from decayed kukui nuts, very vile and foul smelling, and a long stout rope of ieie vines. Ku knew where the door to the Under-world was, a hole near the seashore in the valley of Waipio. Hiku rubbed his body all over with the rancid kukui oil, gave the ieie vine into the keeping of his father, and slowly Ku let the vine down until at last Hiku stood in the strange land of Milu. He rubbed his body once more thoroughly with the oil and disfigured himself with dirt; as he passed from place to place searching for Kewalu the ghosts said, 'What a bad-smelling spirit!' and turned away from him as if he were one of the most unworthy ghosts dwelling in Milu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the realm of Milu he saw the people in the game of rolling cocoanut-shells to hit a post; Kulioe had lost all his property to the daughter of Milu, and saw Hiku: 'If you are a skilful man perhaps you should play with these two girls.' Kulioe bet his bones; Hiku swung the cup, and it glided and twisted around the floor and struck the post, counting five and winning the first bet; then he threw the cup numbered twenty, won all the property and gave it back to Kulioe. At last he found Kewalu by the side of the high chief Milu, who had seen the beautiful princess as she came into the Under-world and called her at once to the highest place in his court. While she was singing her mele the people were startled to hear a clear voice chanting the response which was known by no other person but Hiku. She wandered from place to place looking for Hiku; the only one very close was a foul-smelling, dirt-covered ghost, and Hiku in a low tone warned her to be very careful and not recognize him, but assured her that he had come in person to rescue her and take her back to her old home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Hiku came to the place where the vine was hanging he took hold to see if Ku was still carefully guarding the other end; having made himself sure of the aid of the god, he tied the end into a strong loop and seated himself in it, beginning to swing back and forth, sometimes rising high and sometimes resting with his feet on the ground. Kewalu came near and begged to be allowed to swing; he would only consent on the condition that she would sit in his lap. The ghosts thought this would be an excellent arrangement and shouted their approval. Then Hiku took the spirit of Kewalu in his strong arms and began to swing slowly, then more and more rapidly, higher and higher, while he gave the signal to Ku to pull them up; almost imperceptibly the swing receded from the spirit world. All this time he had been gently rubbing the spirit and softly uttering charm after charm, so that while they were swaying in the air she was growing smaller and smaller. Suddenly it dawned upon some of the beholders that the vine was being drawn up to the Upper-world: the cry arose, 'He is stealing the woman!' The Under-world was in a great uproar; some of the ghosts leaped as high as they could, others called for Hiku to return, others uttered charms to cause his downfall; but no one could leap high enough to touch Hiku, and the power of all the charms was defeated by the god Ku, who rapidly drew the vine upward. Hiku succeeded in charming the ghost of Kewalu into the cocoanut-shell and stopping the opening tight with his fingers, so that the spirit could not escape, and brought her back to the land of mortals. The spirits of the dead must find their way back little by little through the body from the feet to the eyes; Hiku knelt at the feet, cold and stiff in death, placed the small hole in the end of the shell against the tender spot in the bottom of one of the cold feet, removed his finger and uttered the incantations which would allure the ghost into the body. Little by little the soul of Kewalu came back, and the body grew warm from the feet upward, until at last the eyes opened and the soul looked out upon the blessed life restored to it by the skill and bravery of Hiku.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Gods and Ghosts, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.
